solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: TV viewed outside many shops accepting credit

indicators.note: 'viewed outside' tells us the word for viewed wraps round what follows

parts.note: viewed means seen
a mall holds many shops; plural to match, the shops taking the credit alongside
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A television showing in a shopping centre window, with the stores happy to take credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viewed outside' makes the participle the wrapper, split after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Television is commonly called the small screen, as against the big screen of cinema.

clue.text: Not turning to cut south, going west before old heritage site

indicators.note: the reversed word slices into the rearranged letters of south
going west is taken as going wrong, so the letters of south are rearranged
turning means the word Not is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone refusing to turn back south, heading west towards an ancient monument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going west' means going wrong, so it signals an anagram (SUTHO); 'turning' makes TON. SUTTON HOO is the Anglo-Saxon ship-burial site in Suffolk, England.
explanation.definitionFit: This Suffolk ship burial is one of England's most celebrated archaeological sites, now in National Trust care.

clue.text: By the way, stay in Faroes off and on?

indicators.note: the support word sits inside the selected letters
take letters of Faroes alternately, skipping one, keeping the next

parts.note: a stay is a prop, a support

explanation.surface: A traveller asks whether they are staying in the Faroe Islands intermittently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off and on' picks A, O, S from Faroes; PROP goes inside to give A-PROP-OS.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos is a French-derived conversational aside meaning incidentally, on that subject.

clue.text: Estate feeding game outside new resort

indicators.note: the estate word is fed into the middle of the game
the board game goes round the abbreviation for new

parts.note: Ludo is a board game
an estate is land

explanation.surface: An estate supplying food for game birds out beyond a new holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' suggests shooting birds but is a board game. LLANDUDNO is a Victorian seaside resort in North Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Llandudno is a well-known seaside resort town on the North Wales coast.

clue.text: Semi-changeable island

indicators.note: semi means half, so only the first half of the synonym is kept

parts.note: capricious means fickle, changeable

explanation.surface: An island described as only partly unpredictable.
explanation.walkthrough: The first five of the ten letters of CAPRICIOUS give the Italian island.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is an island in the Bay of Naples, Italy.

clue.text: British man wept pointlessly over little beast

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the whole string is turned upwards

parts.note: a man is a male

indicators.note: PT, short for point, is removed from wept

explanation.surface: A British man sheds tears to no purpose over a small creature.
explanation.walkthrough: WEPT without PT is WE; B + MALE + WE reads upwards as EWE-LAMB.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewe lamb is a young female sheep, a small animal.

clue.text: Sneak affair after regular visits in canteen

indicators.note: calling at the letters at regular intervals picks every other one

explanation.surface: A furtive romance carried on through routine trips to the mess hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Every second letter of SNEAK AFFAIR spells NAAFI, the British forces' canteen organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: The NAAFI runs shops and canteens for the British armed forces, so its name stands for a services canteen.

clue.text: Around end of Lent, make fast or move fast

indicators.note: the mooring word goes round the chosen letter

parts.note: to moor a boat is to make it fast

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of Lent

explanation.surface: Advice about Lent: should one keep the fast or hurry along?
explanation.walkthrough: 'make fast' looks like religious fasting but is mooring a boat; MOOR wraps T to give MOTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: To motor is informal for to travel quickly, to speed along.

clue.text: It's used to sum up outrageous hammiest act

indicators.note: outrageous suggests wildness, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A ham actor's most overblown performance is used to sum up their career.
explanation.definitionFit: Mathematics is the discipline of calculation, the subject used to add things up.

clue.text: Don't upset this old man, returning with outline record for retirement

indicators.note: returning means the word for old man is read backwards

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so this pair is read backwards

parts.note: to trace is to outline
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: Advice not to upset an elderly father coming back with a sketched record for his retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: AP, then TRACE + LP backwards (PLECART), gives APPLE-CART.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'upset the applecart' means spoil a plan, so this is the thing one should not upset.

clue.text: Maybe Westwood runs in to take care of me

indicators.note: the runs letter goes into the caring word

parts.note: to tend is to take care of
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
the compiler, a crossword setter, refers to themselves

explanation.surface: A golfer named Westwood dashes in to look after the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Westwood' suggests golfer Lee Westwood, but it is fashion designer Vivienne Westwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Vivienne Westwood was a fashion designer who led styles, an example of a pioneer of fashion.

clue.text: Marched or walked round eastern Europe

indicators.note: the walking word goes round the letters that follow

parts.note: trod is the past of tread, walked
the eastern end of the word Europe is its last three letters, OPE

explanation.surface: Troops marched, or simply walked, around Eastern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eastern' takes the right-hand end of the word Europe, as on a map, and 'round' sends TROD around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trooped means moved along in a body, as soldiers march in formation.

clue.text: Assume current puzzle is rejected following month's late delivery

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

indicators.note: the month letter is delivered to a different spot in the reversed word
rejected means the puzzle word is turned back

parts.note: an enigma is a puzzle
M is the abbreviation for month

explanation.surface: Someone assumes a current puzzle was turned down because of a month's late delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is rejected' gives AMGINE; 'late delivery' shifts the M so it arrives at the front instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To imagine can mean to suppose or take for granted, a synonym of assume.

clue.text: Distinctive character embraced by Internet host

indicators.note: the answer sits held inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A distinctive personality welcomed by a website's host.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethos means the characteristic spirit or values of a group or culture.

clue.text: Confound committee panel in 7 Across

parts.note: 'dash it!' is a mild curse, like 'confound it!'
a board is a governing committee

explanation.surface: Annoyance with a committee panel inside a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 Across is MOTOR, a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The dashboard is the instrument panel at the front of a car's interior.

clue.text: Hide a source of Sparks who'll never 22

parts.note: an animal's hide is its skin
flint struck with steel gives off sparks; Sparks is also the setter's name

explanation.surface: The setter Sparks seems to hide from paying up.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 Across is FORK OUT, pay reluctantly; 'Sparks' doubles as the setter's own pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser never wants to pay up, so someone who will never part with money is tight-fisted.

clue.text: Cause of falling pressure in top-notch projectile

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written here with I for the 1

indicators.note: the pressure letter goes inside the combined pieces

parts.note: a rocket is a projectile
P is the physics abbreviation for pressure

explanation.surface: A first-rate projectile under pressure might come down.
explanation.walkthrough: Top-notch is A1, written with the letter I standing for the figure 1.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket of turbulent air can make an aircraft drop suddenly.

clue.text: Disheartened Iraqi orator reforms, introducing force more conclusively

indicators.note: the force letter is brought into the rearranged letters
reforms means the letters are reshaped
with its heart gone, only the outer letters of Iraqi remain

parts.note: F is the physics abbreviation for force

explanation.surface: A disheartened Iraqi speaker reforms, pressing the argument all the more strongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforms' rearranges the outer letters of Iraqi with orator into AORTIORI; 'introducing' brings F in after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortiori is Latin for 'from the stronger argument', meaning with even greater reason.

clue.text: That is out of order, appearing after time limit

indicators.note: the rest follows the time abbreviation

parts.note: a computer system that is down is out of order

explanation.surface: Something broken coming after a deadline.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie down is to restrict or constrain someone, to limit them.

clue.text: Double prize-winner, one entering preserve

indicators.note: the numeral goes into the preserving word

parts.note: to cure meat is to preserve it
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A twice-honoured champion goes into preserving.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes, in physics and chemistry.

clue.text: Brains of Britain caught before going ahead with answer

indicators.note: the caught-before pair goes ahead of the Britain abbreviation

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: Britain's best minds, caught out before they could press ahead with an answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going ahead' puts caught-before in front, though the clue mentions Britain first.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerebra is the Latin-derived plural of cerebrum, the main part of the brain.

clue.text: Entrance old French painter with dominant element of expressionism

parts.note: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a 19th-century French painter
S is the commonest letter in the word expressionism, appearing three times

explanation.surface: A doorway to a French master's gallery, featuring Expressionist work.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingress means the act or way of going in, an entry.

clue.text: Despondency of union member after swapping sides?

indicators.note: the R for right changes sides to L for left

parts.note: a marriage is a union, and the bridegroom is one partner
R stands for right
L stands for left

explanation.surface: A trade unionist who crossed the floor feels low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'union member' suggests a trade union, but it is a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloom is a state of dejection or low spirits.

clue.text: Food mentioned in petition by female

indicators.note: mentioned means spoken, so we want the sound of the words

parts.note: to sue is to petition, and she is a female

explanation.surface: A meal referred to in a woman's petition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is Japanese rice-based cuisine, a kind of food.

clue.text: Pay reluctantly because of fine, about to get extremely upset

parts.note: for can mean because of, as in 'jumped for joy'

indicators.note: about turns the word for fine round

parts.note: OK means fine

indicators.note: extremely means take the extreme letters, the first and last

explanation.surface: Someone pays up grudgingly for a fine, about to lose their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: To fork out is the idiom for handing over money, usually unwillingly.

clue.text: Runner fell into place going before former baton holder?

indicators.note: the first part precedes the runner
the felling abbreviation goes inside the placing word

parts.note: to stow is to place or put away
KO, knockout, is to fell an opponent
a ski is a runner on snow

explanation.surface: An athlete fell and ended up running before a former relay baton holder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' and 'baton' suggest athletics. Leopold Stokowski often conducted without a baton, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Stokowski was a famous twentieth-century orchestra conductor, and conductors wield batons.

clue.text: Financier having name-dropped one who produces waffle?

indicators.note: the name abbreviation is dropped from the money word

parts.note: a banker is a financier

explanation.surface: A financier who name-drops talks nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waffle' looks like idle talk, but it is a batter cake that a baker makes.
explanation.definitionFit: Waffles are baked goods, so a maker of them is a baker; the question mark flags the pun.

clue.text: Gathered to catch moving trains by main route in a channel

indicators.note: the gathering word catches the following letters inside

parts.note: met means gathered together

indicators.note: moving means the letters of trains are shifted around

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, written AI

explanation.surface: People gathered to see moving trains by the main road to a sea channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges trains to NAISTR. The A1 is the Great North Road, Britain's main north-south route, written AI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Menai Strait is the channel separating Anglesey from mainland Wales.
